sections.h2: What is it like to sell a house in Winston-Salem, NC?
sections.html:
Winston-Salem is the largest of the four cities in this group, and its housing market is more owner-driven and more moderately priced than the coastal cities in the state. The Census Bureau estimates 257,271 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 3.1% from the 2020 base, spread over 132.68 square miles of land.

That size means a seller can face very different conditions block by block: a restored home in a historic neighborhood, a mid-century ranch, a rental that tenants have worn down, or an inherited house in need of work. The right route depends on what the house needs and how fast you need to close.

  • A traditional listing works best when the house shows well and you can handle repairs and inspections.
  • An as-is sale to an investor or cash buyer suits houses with deferred maintenance, code problems or tenants.
  • A sale after probate needs the estate paperwork finished first, since the personal representative signs the deed.

sections.h2: What do Census numbers say about Winston-Salem housing?
sections.html:
Winston-Salem is a majority-owner city with mid-range values. The 2020-2024 Census figures show 55.6% of homes owner-occupied, a median owner-occupied home value of $233,800 and median gross rent of $1,087.

Household data adds context. The city has 103,058 households averaging 2.35 people, 15.4% of residents are 65 or older and median household income is $59,268. Those figures point to a mix of families, retirees and renters, which is the pool of buyers and tenants that any listing here draws from.

sections.h2: How did Winston-Salem form, and why does it matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Winston-Salem was two towns before it was one city. The city's own history pages cover Salem from 1763 to 1913, Winston from 1849 to 1913 and the combined city from 1913 onward, and the city's bicycle plan names tobacco, through R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Company, as the primary industry after founding.

That layered past shows up in the housing stock. The city lists National Register properties in the county that include the Ardmore Historic District, the Arista Cotton Mill Complex and the Bethabara and Bethania historic districts, among many more. Owners of old houses may find buyers who value the character, but also lenders and insurers who ask about wiring, plumbing and roofs.

If your house is in a designated district, ask the city's planning staff what exterior approvals buyers would need before you advertise it as renovation-ready.

sections.h2: Who handles permits and housing code problems in Winston-Salem?
sections.html:
The Inspections Division of the Planning and Development Services Department handles them. It is a city-county agency that reviews and inspects building and zoning activity across Forsyth County except in High Point, Kernersville and King, and it enforces the zoning codes of Winston-Salem, Forsyth County, Clemmons, Lewisville and Walkertown.

The city also keeps a distressed properties page listing houses with housing code violations that could be referred to City Council for demolition if they are not brought into compliance. A house with open violations is harder to sell on the retail market, because lenders and inspectors flag it.

  • Call the Inspections Division at 336-727-2624 to ask about open permits or violations on your address.
  • Fix or document safety violations before listing, or disclose them to a cash buyer up front.
  • Do not pay invoices that arrive by email claiming to come from the city or county. The division warns that these are fake and that payments are made inside its own system.

sections.h2: Who sends the property tax bill in Winston-Salem?
sections.html:
Forsyth County does. The Forsyth County Tax Assessor and Collector administers property tax for the county, Winston-Salem, Clemmons, Kernersville, Lewisville and several other towns, so a single bill covers county and city levies. Bills for real estate and personal property go out in July, and a bill that has not arrived by September 15 is a reason to call the collector.

Tax is due September 1 and payable through January 5, moving to the next business day when January 5 lands on a weekend. After that, the office charges 2% for January and three-quarters of one percent for each later month. The collector accepts cash, checks, money orders, cashier's checks, and online or phone payment with a convenience fee. Mailed payments count by the USPS postmark, and the office suggests mailing five business days early.

The Forsyth tax collector's page flags an important change from North Carolina Session Law 2006-106: if tax is unpaid after January 5, the owner on January 6 becomes liable. For a seller, that means an unpaid bill can follow the property to the buyer, so ask the closing attorney to pay current-year tax at closing.

sections.h2: How often does Forsyth County reappraise, and how do you appeal?
sections.html:
Forsyth County reappraises more often than the state minimum. State law requires every eighth year, and the county says it has generally reappraised every four years since 1988. The 2025 reappraisal took effect January 1, 2025, replacing values set in 2021, so the change on your notice reflects four years of market movement.

The county's appeal form for the Board of Equalization and Review states that all property is appraised at 100% of fair market value. In the usual process, you ask for an informal review, then a hearing before the board. The state's later steps follow in order: a written notice of appeal to the Property Tax Commission within 30 days after the board mails its decision.

  • Collect sales of similar nearby houses and any recent appraisal.
  • Photograph damage that the county's records do not show.
  • Remember that values reflect the property as it stood on January 1.

Ask the Forsyth tax office for the current year's board deadlines, because they change with the calendar.

sections.h2: What tax relief and closing costs apply in Winston-Salem?
sections.html:
Three state programs may lower the tax on a permanent residence, and an owner may use only one. The elderly or disabled exclusion removes the greater of $25,000 or half the appraised value; the disabled veteran exclusion removes the first $45,000; and the circuit breaker limits tax to 4% or 5% of income with the unpaid portion deferred as a lien. Deferred tax becomes due on a transfer, so selling triggers repayment. The NC Department of Revenue prints the 2026 income limit as $38,800, and applications go to the county tax assessor, who must accept them through June 1.

At closing, the seller pays the deed excise tax at $1.00 per $500 of value, collected by the register of deeds before recording. Standard recording runs $26 for the first 15 pages and $64 for a deed of trust, plus $4 per added page.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Winston-Salem house with code violations?
faqs.a: Yes, but expect a lower price or a buyer who takes it as-is. The city lists houses with housing code violations that could be referred to council for demolition. Call the Inspections Division at 336-727-2624 to learn what is open on your address.

faqs.q: When are Forsyth County property taxes due?
faqs.a: They are due September 1 and payable through January 5. Interest starts after that date: 2% in January and three-quarters of one percent each month after. If January 5 falls on a weekend, the deadline moves to the next business day.

faqs.q: Who owes unpaid tax if I sell after the bill is mailed?
faqs.a: The owner on the day the tax becomes past due is liable under Session Law 2006-106, as the county collector's page explains. Normally the buyer and seller prorate at closing. Ask your closing attorney to pay the tax from the sale proceeds.

faqs.q: How often does Forsyth County revalue homes?
faqs.a: Roughly every four years. The county says it has reappraised that often since 1988, and the latest took effect January 1, 2025. State law sets eight years as the longest allowed gap.

faqs.q: Does Winston-Salem charge a transfer tax?
faqs.a: North Carolina charges a state excise tax of $1.00 per $500 of consideration, paid by the seller to the register of deeds. The Forsyth pages opened for this guide list no separate city transfer tax. Ask your closing attorney to confirm the total.
